docs.text:
I break into systems so the people who own them don't have to find out the hard way.

I'm a cybersecurity student at Old Dominion University and a working penetration tester, focused on web application security and FedRAMP red team assessments. Most of my work is running authorized tests against web apps and network services with Burp Suite, Metasploit, and Kali Linux, then assessing cloud environments with ScoutSuite. I care as much about the write-up as the exploit, since a finding nobody understands doesn't get fixed. I'm looking for offensive security work where proving the risk is the whole job.

docs.title: What I do
docs.text:
I run authorized penetration tests against web applications and network services, working primarily in Kali Linux with Burp Suite for application testing and Metasploit for exploitation and post-exploitation. On the cloud side I assess AWS environments with ScoutSuite and write the findings up in a form an engineering team can act on.

The coursework behind that spans offensive security, network and wireless security, cryptography, and the legal and regulatory frameworks that decide what a test is allowed to touch. The projects below are the evidence.

An AWS security review using ScoutSuite, covering IAM, S3, EBS, and load balancer configuration, plus a written finding on an API token weakness.

03 Offensive Security Labs

Hands-on exploitation work. Password cracking with John the Ripper and Hashcat, Windows post-exploitation with Meterpreter, and Linux privilege and account management.

IEEE 802.11 security, RF propagation, switch hierarchy, DNSSEC, and an analysis of where VPN implementations actually fail.

05 Cybersecurity and Society

The human side. Breach analysis of Equifax, IoT risk, and coursework applying behavioral and criminological models to how people and systems fail.

06 Incident Response Simulation

Detection, analysis, containment, and recovery against a simulated intrusion, with the methodology and the decision points written down.

docs.title: Where I am headed

I want to keep working on the offensive side, specifically web application assessments and red team engagements against federal and FedRAMP-scoped environments. That work rewards people who can find the flaw and then explain it clearly enough that somebody fixes it, which is the part I care about.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
I'm a cybersecurity student and a working penetration tester based in Spotsylvania, VA, available for remote work.

Most of what I do is offensive security. I run authorized penetration tests against web apps and network services: scope the engagement, find vulnerabilities, prove it, write it up. The write-up matters as much as the finding, since a vulnerability nobody understands doesn't get remediated.

My coursework goes directly into the work rather than being useless. Offensive security, network and wireless security, cryptography, and cloud security all show up in what I actually do day to day. The legal and regulatory material sets the boundaries for what a test is allowed to touch and the criminology courses have turned out more useful than expected. Most breaches come down to someone making a bad call under pressure, not some novel exploit.

docs.title: How I work
docs.text:
I am most useful on engagements where the goal is depth rather than coverage. I would rather fully understand one exploitable path and document it properly than produce a scanner export with two hundred low-severity items in it.

I also try to stay honest about the limits of a test. A finding I could not reproduce goes in the report as exactly that. Overstating a result costs you credibility the first time somebody checks your work.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Six areas, each with what I actually do in it. Where a skill is still developing I have said so rather than padding the list.

docs.title: 01. Web application penetration testing
docs.text:
My primary focus. Authorized testing against web applications using Burp Suite for interception, request manipulation, and scanning, working out of Kali Linux. Covers the standard application attack surface, including injection, broken access control, authentication and session handling, and insecure direct object references.

The output is a reproducible finding. Request, response, impact, and the minimum steps another tester needs to confirm it.

docs.title: 02. Network service exploitation and post-exploitation
docs.text:
Exploitation of network services with Metasploit, and Windows post-exploitation using Meterpreter, including privilege escalation, credential access, and persistence in a lab environment.

Also covers Linux account and permission management, which is less exciting than exploitation but is where a surprising number of real findings come from.

docs.title: 03. Credential attacks
docs.text:
Offline password cracking with John the Ripper and Hashcat, including hash identification, wordlist and rule-based attacks, and reasoning about how long a given hash type actually takes to break with the hardware available.

The practical takeaway from this work is that password policy advice is mostly wrong, and that hash algorithm choice matters more than complexity rules.

docs.title: 04. Cloud security assessment
docs.text:
AWS environment review using ScoutSuite, covering IAM policy and role configuration, S3 bucket exposure, EBS volume encryption, and load balancer settings. Comfortable reading the output critically rather than exporting it whole, since a scanner result is a starting point and not a finding.

Includes writing up cryptographic weaknesses found in application code, such as API tokens generated with MD5.

docs.title: 05. Network and wireless security
docs.text: IEEE 802.11 security mechanisms and their failure modes, RF propagation and how it affects real coverage and interception range, switch hierarchy and segmentation, DNSSEC, and where VPN implementations break down in practice.

docs.title: 06. Security writing and reporting
docs.text:
The part that makes the rest of it useful. Writing findings that a developer or a system owner can act on without having to interpret them, separating severity from urgency, and giving remediation guidance that fits the system being tested rather than generic advice.

This extends to regulatory context. Knowing which framework applies, FedRAMP or CMMC or otherwise, changes what a finding means to the organization receiving it.

docs.title: Cloud Security Assessment
docs.text: PlatformAmazon Web Services Primary toolScoutSuite ScopeIAM, S3, EBS, ALB OutputWritten findings

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Cloud misconfiguration is a different problem from a software vulnerability. There is usually no exploit to write. The service is working exactly as configured, and the configuration is the flaw. That changes how you assess it and how you report it.

This assessment reviewed an AWS environment for configuration weaknesses across identity, storage, compute, and network-facing services.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
I used ScoutSuite to enumerate the environment and produce an initial picture, then worked through the results by hand. A scanner tells you what is technically true. It does not tell you what matters in the context of the account, and it produces findings that are accurate but not meaningful.

Areas reviewed:

  • IAM. Policy and role configuration, permission scope, and trust relationships that were broader than what was required.
  • S3. Bucket exposure and access policy, including public access settings and encryption at rest.
  • EBS. Volume encryption coverage across attached and detached volumes.
  • Application Load Balancer. Listener configuration and TLS settings.

docs.title: Why this is on a technical portfolio
docs.text: Because the technical explanation of a breach is usually the least interesting part of it. The vulnerability is the mechanism. The reason it stayed unpatched, or the reason nobody escalated the alert, is the actual cause. This coursework is about that second half.

docs.title: Equifax breach analysis
docs.text:
Research into the 2017 Equifax breach. The initial vector was a known vulnerability in Apache Struts with a patch available before the intrusion. The technical finding is a single sentence, and it explains almost nothing on its own.

What is worth studying is the organizational failure around it. How a patch with a published advisory went unapplied, how the intrusion went undetected for as long as it did, and what that says about the difference between having a vulnerability management process and having one that works.

docs.title: IoT security risk
docs.text: Analysis of the security posture of consumer and industrial IoT. The recurring problems are structural rather than individual. Devices ship with default credentials, have no practical update mechanism, stay deployed for a decade, and are built by manufacturers with no incentive to support them past the warranty period.

docs.title: Human factors
docs.text:
Coursework applying behavioral models to security, including work applying Maslow's hierarchy of needs to how people relate to technology, and criminological theory covering strain theories, deterrence research, and biological explanations of offending.

The connection to the day job is direct. Deterrence research in particular tells you something uncomfortable about security controls, which is that the certainty of being caught changes behavior far more than the severity of the consequence. That has implications for how you design monitoring, and it argues against a lot of common policy.
